{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
In the [[mathematics]] of [[dynamical systems]], the concept of '''Lyapunov dimension''' was suggested by [[Kaplan–Yorke conjecture|Kaplan and Yorke]]<ref name=KaplanY-1979>{{cite book
 | author = Kaplan J., Yorke J. 
 | year = 1979
 | title = Chaotic behavior of multidimensional difference equations 
 | chapter = Functional Differential Equations and Approximations of Fixed Points
 | publisher = Springer
 | pages = 204–227
}}</ref> for estimating the [[Hausdorff dimension]] of [[attractor]]s. 
Further the concept has been developed and rigorously justified in a number of papers, and nowadays various different approaches to the definition of Lyapunov dimension are used. Attractors with noninteger Hausdorff dimension are called [[Attractor#Strange attractor|strange attractors]].<ref name=RuelleT-1971>{{cite journal
 |author1=Ruelle D. |author2=Takens F. |year = 1971
 | title = On the nature of turbulence
 | journal = Communications in Mathematical Physics
 | volume = 20
 | number = 3
 | pages = 167–192
 | doi=10.1007/bf01646553
|bibcode=1971CMaPh..20..167R }}</ref> Since the direct [[numerical analysis|numerical computation]] of the Hausdorff dimension of attractors is often a problem of high numerical complexity, estimations via the Lyapunov dimension became widely spread.
The Lyapunov dimension was named<ref name=FredericksonKYY-1983>{{cite journal
 | last1=Frederickson | first1=F. 
 | last2=Kaplan | first2=J. 
 | last3=Yorke | first3=E. 
 | last4=Yorke | first4=J. 
 | title=The Liapunov dimension of strange attractors
 | journal=Journal of Differential Equations
 | volume=49 | issue=2 | pages=185–207
 | year=1983 | doi=10.1016/0022-0396(83)90011-6
 | bibcode=1983JDE....49..185F 
 | doi-access=free}}</ref> after the Russian mathematician [[Aleksandr Lyapunov]] because of the close connection with the [[Lyapunov exponents]].

==Definitions==
Consider a [[dynamical system]]  
<math> \big(\{\varphi^t\}_{t\geq0}, (U\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n, \|\cdot\|)\big) </math>, where <math>\varphi^t</math> is the [[shift operator]] along the solutions:
<math> \varphi^t(u_0) = u(t,u_0)</math>,
of [[Ordinary differential equation|ODE]] <math>\dot{u} = f({u})</math>, <math> t \leq 0</math>,  
or difference equation <math>{u}(t+1) = f({u}(t))</math>, <math> t=0,1,...</math>,
with continuously differentiable vector-function <math>f</math>.
Then <math>D\varphi^t(u)</math> is the [[Fundamental matrix (linear differential equation)|fundamental matrix of solutions]] of linearized system
and denote by <math>\sigma_i(t,u) = \sigma_i(D\varphi^t(u)), \ i = 1...n</math>,
[[singular values]] with respect to their [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors#Algebraic multiplicity|algebraic multiplicity]],
ordered by decreasing for any <math>u</math> and <math>t</math>.

===Definition via finite-time Lyapunov dimension===
The concept of '''finite-time Lyapunov dimension''' and related definition of the Lyapunov dimension, developed in the works by [[Nikolay_V._Kuznetsov|N.&nbsp;Kuznetsov]],<ref name=Kuznetsov-2016-PLA>{{Cite journal |first=N.V. |last=Kuznetsov |title=The Lyapunov dimension and its estimation via the Leonov method |journal=Physics Letters A |volume=380 |year=2016 |issue=25–26 |pages=2142–2149 |doi= 10.1016/j.physleta.2016.04.036|bibcode =2016PhLA..380.2142K |arxiv=1602.05410|s2cid=118467839 }}</ref><ref name=KuznetsovLMPS-2018>{{Cite journal
|first1=N.V. |last1=Kuznetsov
|first2=G.A. |last2=Leonov
|first3=T.N. |last3=Mokaev
|first4=A. |last4=Prasad
|first5=M.D. |last5=Shrimali 
|title=Finite-time Lyapunov dimension and hidden attractor of the Rabinovich system
|journal=Nonlinear Dynamics
|volume=92 | issue=2 |year=2018 |pages=267–285 |doi=10.1007/s11071-018-4054-z|arxiv=1504.04723|s2cid=254888463
}}</ref> is convenient for the numerical experiments where only finite time can be observed.
Consider an analog of the [[Kaplan–Yorke conjecture|Kaplan–Yorke formula]] for the finite-time Lyapunov exponents:
:<math>
   d_{\rm KY}(\{ {\rm LE}_i(t,u)\}_{i=1}^n)=j(t,u) + 
   \frac{ {\rm LE}_1(t,u) + \cdots + {\rm LE}_{j(t,u)}(t,u)}{| {\rm LE}_{j(t,u)+1}(t,u)|},
   </math>
:<math>
j(t,u) = \max\{m: \sum_{i=1}^m {\rm LE}_i(t,u) \geq 0\},
</math>
with respect to the ordered set of ''finite-time Lyapunov exponents''
<math>\{{\rm LE}_i(t,u)\}_{i=1}^n = \{\frac{1}{t}\ln\sigma_i(t,u)\}_{i=1}^n</math> at the point <math>u</math>.
The ''finite-time Lyapunov dimension'' of dynamical system with respect
to [[Invariant manifold|invariant set]] <math>K</math>
is defined as follows
:<math>
  \dim_{\rm L}(t, K) = \sup\limits_{u \in K}
  d_{\rm KY}(\{{\rm LE}_i(t,u)\}_{i=1}^n).
</math>

In this approach the use of the analog of Kaplan–Yorke formula
is rigorously justified by the Douady–Oesterlè theorem,<ref name=DouadyO-1980>{{Cite journal
|first1=A. |last1=Douady |author-link=Adrien Douady
|first2=J. |last2=Oesterle
|title=Dimension de Hausdorff des attracteurs
|journal=Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, Série A
|volume=290 | issue=24 |year=1980 |pages=1135–1138}}</ref> which proves that for any fixed <math>t > 0</math>
the ''finite-time Lyapunov dimension'' for a closed bounded invariant set <math>K</math>
is an upper estimate of the Hausdorff dimension:
:<math>
  \dim_{\rm H} K \leq \dim_{\rm L}(t, K).
</math>
Looking for best such estimation 
<math>
\inf_{t>0} \dim_{\rm L} (t, K)
  = \liminf_{t \to +\infty}\sup\limits_{u \in K} \dim_{\rm L}(t,u)
</math>, ''the Lyapunov dimension'' is defined as follows:<ref name=Kuznetsov-2016-PLA/><ref name=KuznetsovLMPS-2018/>
:<math>
  \dim_{\rm L} K = \liminf_{t \to +\infty}\sup\limits_{u \in K} \dim_{\rm L}(t,u).
</math>
The possibilities of changing the order of the time limit and the [[Infimum and supremum|supremum]] over set is discussed, e.g., in.<ref name=ConstantinFT-1985>{{Cite journal
|first1=P.  |last1=Constantin
|first2=C.  |last2=Foias
|first3=R.  | last3=Temam
|title=Attractors representing turbulent flows
|journal=Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society
|volume=53 | issue=314 |year=1985 |pages=1–67|doi=10.1090/memo/0314
}}</ref><ref name=EdenFT-1991>{{Cite journal
|first1=A. |last1=Eden
|first2=C. |last2=Foias
|first3=R. | last3=Temam
|title=Local and global Lyapunov exponents
|journal=Journal of Dynamics and Differential Equations
|volume=3 | issue=1 |year=1991 |pages=133–177 |doi=10.1007/bf01049491|bibcode=1991JDDE....3..133E
|s2cid=119490212
}}</ref>

Note that the above defined Lyapunov dimension is invariant under Lipschitz [[diffeomorphisms]].<ref name=Kuznetsov-2016-PLA/><ref name=KuznetsovAL-2016>{{Cite journal
|first1=N. |last1=Kuznetsov
|first2=T. |last2=Alexeeva
|first3=G. |last3=Leonov
|title=Invariance of Lyapunov exponents and Lyapunov dimension for regular and irregular linearizations
|journal=Nonlinear Dynamics
|volume=85 | issue=1 |year=2016 |pages=195–201 |doi=10.1007/s11071-016-2678-4|arxiv=1410.2016 |s2cid=254894000
}}</ref>

====Exact Lyapunov dimension====
Let the Jacobian matrix <math>Df(u_\text{eq})</math> at one of the equilibria have simple real eigenvalues:
<math>\{\lambda_i(u_\text{eq})\}_{i=1}^n, \lambda_{i}(u_\text{eq}) \geq \lambda_{i+1}(u_\text{eq})</math>,
then 
:<math>
  \dim_{\rm L}u_\text{eq} = d_{\rm KY}(\{\lambda_i(u_\text{eq})\}_{i=1}^n).
</math>
If the supremum of local Lyapunov dimensions on the global attractor, which involves all equilibria, is achieved at an [[Equilibrium point (mathematics)|equilibrium point]], then this allows one to get analytical formula of the exact Lyapunov dimension of the global attractor (see corresponding [[Eden’s conjecture]]).

===Definition via statistical physics approach and ergodicity===
Following the [[statistical physics]] approach and assuming the [[ergodicity]]
the Lyapunov dimension of attractor is estimated<ref name=KaplanY-1979/> by 
limit value of the local Lyapunov dimension <math>\lim_{t\to+\infty}\dim_{\rm L} (t, u_0)</math> 
of a ''typical'' trajectory,  which belongs to the attractor.
In this case <math>\{\lim\limits_{t\to+\infty}{\rm LE}_i(t,u_0)\}_{i}^n = \{ {\rm LE}_i(u_0)\}_1^n</math> 
and <math>\dim_{\rm L}u_0= d_{\rm KY}(\{ {\rm LE}_i(u_0)\}_{i=1}^n)=j(u_0) + \frac{ {\rm LE}_1(u_0) + \cdots + {\rm LE}_{j(u_0)}(u_0)}{| {\rm LE}_{j(u_0)+1}(u_0)|} </math>.
From a practical point of view, the rigorous use of [[Oseledec theorem|ergodic Oseledec theorem]],
verification that the considered trajectory <math>u(t,u_0)</math> is a ''typical'' trajectory, 
and the use of corresponding [[Kaplan–Yorke conjecture|Kaplan–Yorke formula]] is a challenging task
(see, e.g. discussions in<ref name=ChaosBook>{{cite book
 |author1= P. Cvitanovic |author2=R. Artuso |author3=R. Mainieri
 |author4= G. Tanner |author5= G. Vattay  
 |name-list-style=amp | year = 2017
 | title = Chaos: Classical and Quantum
 | publisher = Niels Bohr Institute
 | url = http://chaosbook.org/version15/chapters/Lyapunov.pdf#page=6
 }}</ref>). 
The exact limit values of finite-time Lyapunov exponents,
if they exist and are the same for all <math>u_0 \in U</math>,
are called the ''absolute'' ones<ref name=FredericksonKYY-1983/> <math>\{\lim\limits_{t\to+\infty}{\rm LE}_i(t,u_0)\}_{i}^n = \{ {\rm LE}_i(u_0)\}_1^n \equiv \{ {\rm LE}_i \}_1^n</math> and used in the [[Kaplan–Yorke conjecture|Kaplan–Yorke formula]].
Examples of the rigorous use of the [[ergodic theory]] for the computation of the Lyapunov exponents and dimension can be found in.<ref name=Ledrappier-1981>{{cite journal
 | last1=Ledrappier | first1=F. 
 | title=Some relations between dimension and Lyapounov exponents
 | journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics
 | volume=81 | issue=2 | pages=229–238
 | year=1981
 | doi=10.1007/bf01208896
 | bibcode=1981CMaPh..81..229L 
 | s2cid=122105442 
 | url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1103920241 
 }}</ref><ref name=BenedicksY-1993>{{cite journal
 | last1=Benedicks | first1=M. 
 | last2=Young | first2=L.-S. 
 | title=Sinai–Bowen–Ruelle measures for certain Henon maps
 | journal=Inventiones Mathematicae
 | volume=112 | issue=1 | pages=541–576
 | year=1993 | doi=10.1007/bf01232446
 | bibcode=1993InMat.112..541B 
 }}</ref><ref name=2021-KuznetsovR>{{cite book | first1= Nikolay | last1=Kuznetsov | 
first2=Volker | last2=Reitmann | year = 2021| title = Attractor Dimension Estimates for Dynamical Systems: Theory and Computation| 
publisher = Springer| location = Cham|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783030509866}}</ref>
